newsitem.title: UK: DMG says had duty to suspend Horlick.
newsitem.headline: DMG says had duty to suspend Horlick.

text.p: Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, the investment banking arm of Germany's Deutsche Bank, said on Wednesday that a sense of duty had forced it to suspend fund manager Nicola Horlick.

"We have a duty, unpleasant though it may be, to the firm and to our clients. We would be failing in that duty if we did not investigate this matter," DMG spokesman James Murray told Reuters in response to a question on why it had opted to suspend Horlick rather than sort the matter out internally.

DMG suspended 35-year-old Horlick, head of Morgan Grenfell Asset Management's pension fund business, "pending the outcome of an internal investigation which will look at a potential breach of her contract".
Banking sources said the suspension followed talks between Horlick and Dutch bank ABN AMRO and overtures made by Horlick to members of her team at MGAM to move to the Dutch firm.

Horlick, who was not immediately available for comment, told British newspapers on Tuesday that she was unable to comment on her suspension. And on Wednesday ABN AMRO denied it had any intention of poaching staff from MGAM.

"We are surprised to be mentioned in the context of poaching which would, by its nature, imply you are planning to take a whole team, which we are not," the bank's chief spokesman Jules Prast told Reuters.
But Prast said he preferred not to discuss whether ABN AMRO had talked or planned to talk to Horlick. "We never comment on who we are talking to before anything is concluded," he added.
DMG stressed Horlick's suspension had "nothing to do with the Peter Young affair and there was no suggestion of financial impropriety".

Last year fund manager Young was sacked for gross misconduct and is currently under investigation by Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO) following the discovery of suspect valuations in three MGAM funds. Young has denied any involvement in criminal activity and said he is being made a scapegoat.

The saga has been an embarrassment for DMG and its parent Deutsche Bank, which had to step in with a 180 million pounds ($301.2 million) cash injection after the funds were suspended in September and has since agreed to a 200 million pound compensation package for investors who lost out as a result.
